Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shorter scan times. Deep learning, specifically the use of universal detectors that combine PET and low-dose CT data, has shown significant potential in enhancing the quality of PET images at reduced doses. Nonetheless, this approach relies heavily on training datasets similar to those used for standard-dose PET, including variations in anatomy, and does not account for uncertainties in measurements or data that fall outside of these protocols. As a result, there is a need for new approaches that can effectively handle low-quality and abnormal data without overfitting, particularly for tissues with limited protocols available. To address this challenge, we propose a novel deep learning framework based on physics principles that incorporates multiple modalities, accounts for uncertainties, and includes accommodations for outside distribution data, all while maintaining efficiency and performance. This framework was successfully applied to reduced-dose PET scans, yielding enhanced images quality, with noticeable gains in contrast-to-noise ratio and lesion detectability compared to standard-dose PET, as well as significant reductions in dose requirements. Notably, our method demonstrated robustness in detecting lesions across various anatomical regions and showed minimal protocol-dependent variations, a key advantage over conventional deep learning approaches. Overall, our uncertainty-conscious deep learning framework provides a viable solution for producing high-quality PET images at reduced doses and is potentially applicable to other low-dose imaging problems. Imitation learning has emerged as a prominent approach for training robust and effective policies, as it leverages existing expertise and ensures the learned behavior meets specified standards. However, the majority of imitation learning algorithms developed so far have limitations: many can only learn to replicate mean rewards, adhere to linear constraints, and evade barriers formed by linear functions of the states, which significantly constrains their potential for complex tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel imitation learning framework, named EKMP, which can learn to produce the desired distribution over rewards, nonlinear constraint constraints, and complex state-dependent barriers, thus enabling the learned agent to operate efficiently in diverse, non-linear domains. Moreover, our framework offers multiple advantages over existing methods: it allows the incorporation of expert data related to reward distribution; can enforce nonlinear rigid constraints based on state action pairs; and builds evading barriers around areas with suboptimal behaviors, as well as providing the theoretical bounds on the policy improvement, which results in an efficient and linearly convergent optimization algorithm. Our approach is particularly suitable for visual imitation learning, where the experts' policies are often unknown, and our results demonstrate the superiority of our framework over state-of-the-art algorithms, achieving significant better performance in various complex tasks. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/MiaoChenBerkley/EKMP. Additionally, we introduce an innovative task, the brain implant planning problem, which requires the development of an optimal sequence of actions under uncertain conditions, multiple nonlinear constraints, and complex state-dependent barriers, and demonstrate the applicability of our framework to solve real-world problems of this type. The solutions developed with EKMP outperform the state-of-the-art algorithms by a margin of up to 50%. The expert data used in our experiments is available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/212MYGQdV7Qr9iE9x3Q4Q, and the models pre-trained with our algorithm at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1x5fT7GlhLQrJQD9QD9x9Q. We have examined a two-dimensional Rashba superfluid with attractive interactions and a population imbalance, and found that it supports a spin-singlet topological superfluid phase. Unlike the case without Rashba interaction, we discovered that the Rashba term enables the emergence of a spin-singlet topological superfluid phase, even in the absence of a finite Chern number. Furthermore, we established that this spin-singlet topological superfluid phase can be realized with the Rashba parameter exceeding a certain threshold, and that it exhibits robustness against spatial symmetry-breaking phase transitions. Our analysis also reveals that the Rashba parameter has a dramatic effect on the superfluid's transition points, causing them to be significantly lowered in energy. These findings suggest that Rashba twist can be an effective means of stabilizing a spin-singlet topological superfluid in experiments. We additionally found that the Rashba interaction enables the merging of two separated superfluid phases into one phase, resulting in an interesting "unmerging" transition in the ground state energy as a function of density. We propose that observation of the spin-singlet topological superfluid's robustness or the unmerging transition could provide experimental evidence of its existence. We further analyzed the population imbalance's effect on the spin-singlet topological superfluid, and found that it can be tuned to optimize this phase. We also obtained the phase diagram of the Rashba superfluid with attractive interactions and population imbalance, and demonstrated that it encompasses not just the spin-singlet topological superfluid phase, but also the Rashba flat band and Bose condensate phases. Lastly, we discussed an experimental protocol that could facilitate detection of the spin-singlet topological superfluid in atomic gas experiments. This includes observing the Rashba-affected boson's scattering dynamics and analyzing its spin-singlet nature via parametric heating of the atomic gas. We predicted that this could result in a marked increase in the scattering signal at an energy located in the middle of the Rashba split bands, and that this effect would also lead to a significant change in the amplitude of this signal when varying the Rashba interaction. This detection protocol can be employed to validate our theoretical predictions and gain a deeper understanding of the interplay between Rashba interaction, attractive interactions, and population imbalance in these systems. We provided a detailed description of an experimental setup that could implement this detection protocol, and outlined the instrumentation required to execute it. By utilizing sensitive resistance measurements and careful temperature control, we have found a previously unreported phase transition in doped Lanthanum Cuprates, occurring at very low magnetic fields near the superconducting critical temperature. Observations suggest this event represents a sudden reorganization of the vortex lattice structure, transforming from a hexagonal to a square pattern without altering the underlying crystal properties. Theoretical models predict this transition for any type of superconductor that exhibits a mixed state, but it has been particularly difficult to detect in Cuprates due to their highly sensitive response to magnetic fields. Our discovery was possible because of the unique conditions created by growing very thin samples, which allow for a clearer, more detailed analysis of the resistance measurements at the critical temperature point. As a result of this finding, we anticipate that it could provide a basis for further exploration of the interplay between different types of fluctuations in these materials. The described phase transition, characterized by a sudden change in the spatial arrangement of superconducting currents at very low magnetic fields near the critical temperature, results in a noticeable resistance minimum and creates an opportunity for further modifying the structure by increasing the level of doping. Additionally, the resistance minimum associated with this transition is susceptible to malformation when certain types of defects are present, as it is for the more well-known resistance minimum associated with the pseudo-gap and it may be reset to its original value by increasing the level of doping. The location of this transition in the phase diagram is in alignment with predictions made by models that explain the physics of the pseudo-gap and it is expected that this finding could provide a path for the observation of the proposed vortex lattice transitions in other types of materials. The precise conditions created by growing very thin samples, that is a high level of sensitivity to magnetic fields combined with a high level of superconducting volume, suggests that the detection of this transition could be achievable with better sensitivity in future measurements of more common types of materials. The serial dictatorship is a well-known mechanism for allocating multiple items among a set of candidates, where the order of selection is determined by their arrival time. It guarantees fairness but may not promote efficiency. A more effective mechanism, the efficient serial dictatorship, is obtained by reordering the candidates based on their individual marginal values of each item, resulting in both fairness and efficiency. This paper introduces the concept of enhancing over serial dictatorships (EoSD) to improve the efficacy of serial dictatorships through item-dependent candidate orderings, without altering the arrival time-based decision rule. It is proven that any EoSD mechanism leads to a socially efficient allocation, although it may compromise some candidates' chances of selection. To address this potential issue, a new fairness criterion, called strong ex- post fairness, is defined to prevent the unfair treatment of candidates in extreme cases. It is shown that no mechanism can satisfy both efficiency and strong ex- post fairness in the case of three or more items. Nonetheless, a fair and efficient solution is achievable when there are only two items available. The paper explores various applications and raises new research questions in the area of mechanism design. It also provides theoretical hardness for some of its problems. Several of its results are based on novel proofs of fair and efficient allocations for specific cases. Moreover, it introduces new item-dependent orderings of candidates that could be useful in other applications. Primarily composed of two objects orbiting a shared center of gravity, binary asteroids offer astronomers a unique opportunity to study asteroid formation and the properties of their collisions. By analyzing images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, researchers found 25 potential binary asteroids among the top rankings for their distinct light curve patterns. Calculations of their rotational periods and pole orientations yielded various collision angles ranging from 15 degrees to 160 degrees, indicating most binary asteroids in this study formed at a relatively shallow angle similar to that of nearby main-belt asteroid (16) Psyche. Additionally, by accounting for light that is blocked or bent as a result of the binary nature, researchers were able to observe the smaller component of one asteroid, (14428) Bopesse, and estimate its size. Further study is needed to confirm the binary status of the 25 candidates and to explore how collision angles of asteroids vary. Systematic observation of these binary asteroids is also crucial to understanding how collisions on asteroids produce moons. Moreover, researchers found that one of these binary asteroids, (12104) Sonni, is actually a binary asteroid with two large components, one that is likely a partially destroyed asteroid that was broken apart by the gravitational pull of the primary body. This is a first-of-its-kind finding for asteroids in the inner main belt. Additionally, (12104) Sonni's collision angle is estimated to be one of the widest ever recorded for a binary asteroid in this region, at approximately 180 degrees. This breakthrough was made possible by combining observations from the Pan-STARRS1 and Gaia spacecraft, with a special approach to solve for the radius of the primary component before being confirmed by ground-based observations. This new finding and approach set the stage for further discovery of multiple component asteroids through analysis of high-quality positional and photometric data from surveys such as the Gaia and upcoming LSST. This is to be expected, given that about one in ten asteroids with a high ranking for their light curve patterns are expected to be binary asteroids with two large components, and that the collision angle of one such asteroid in the outer main-belt was recently determined by researchers. This new field of study offers a unique way to study asteroid formation and collisions, and it highlights the value of optical observations that provide information on an asteroid's shape, rotational period, pole orientation, collision angle, and multiple components, all of which are all essential for a comprehensive understanding of these small bodies in our solar system. A distinct volcanic zone in the Southern Atlantic, where Iceland and South America meet, has been the subject of limited geophysical exploration due to its remote location. However, recent studies using airborne gravity measurements have revealed a previously unseen volcanic ring plain, approximately 1600km in diameter, located near the sea floor where the depth drops to around 2000m. This feature, named the Southern Atlantic fissure (SAF), has been estimated to have formed over 10 million years ago. It exhibits low topography with a central rise, averaging 50-100m in height, and has several large troughs and numerous smaller fissure system fragments. Data from seismic measurements suggest that the SAF is a low-speed geologic area, consistent with the presence of slow basal debris and little evidence of past lubricating mantle plumes. Instead, it shares geophysical characteristics with other volcanic zones in the Atlantic, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge System. Models of plate motion indicate that the SAF is an active and expanding ring plain, with volcanic activity occurring at its periphery. It is believed that this ring plain forms as a result of the interaction between two segments of the South American plate and the Antarctic plate, where Iceland and South America meet. It has been proposed that this could provide a source for the enigmatic Heinrich events, which involved large quantities of freshwater being released, although further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between the SAF and these events. Word meaning changes can be categorized into three types: synonomy, hyponymy, and antonymy. 
Existing studies on word sense induction consider a word's semantic changes acceptable 
if the new meaning is a synonym of the original. 
However, this view overlooks more complex semantic shifts such as hyponymy and antonymy. 
For instance, the word "child" can refer to an underage human but a "youth" is not necessarily 
an underage human. 
Current approaches classify a word as changed semantically if its new context set 
does not overlap with the original context set. 
This thesis introduces three novel metrics that account for a word's semantic shifts. 
One measures the smallest context set that includes both the original and new context sets. 
Another assesses the pragmatism of a word by comparing its original and new context sets 
based on the average of their respective similarity values. 
The third novel metric compares a word's semantic change to the semantic change of a 
known base word. 
To validate these metrics, this research uses three existing word sense inventories. 
One set of experiments classifies a word's semantic change based on its related words. 
Another set of experiments, conducted on texts with annotated time stamps, examines a 
word's semantic change over time. 
For both types of experiments, this research finds that a word's semantic change can 
be detected using a neural network with a document representation method. 
One such method is the Multi-View Neural Network, which achieves an accuracy of 62.5% 
in classifying a word's semantic change based on its related words and an accuracy 
of 57.5% in classifying a word's semantic change over time.

This discovery provides initial insights into the relationship between native states and unfolding routes and sets the stage for further exploration of the interplay between geometry, dynamics, and evolution in proteins. The findings presented here are based on simulations of 25 unique protein knots and their corresponding mirror images, encompassing nearly half of all possible knot types. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on accurate individual predictions, but existing methods typically operate on isolated datasets, neglecting the potential of collaborative learning. In response, we present a novel technique called FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework for healthcare on wearable devices. FedHealth enables the sharing of knowledge and collaborative prediction on decentralized datasets by utilizing linear transformations to align data from different users. We conclude that FedHealth achieves comparable performance to standalone training and outperforms other transfer learning approaches by testing it on three open-source datasets involving activity recognition, sleep duration, and sport activity prediction. Furthermore, we find that FedHealth's performance is comparable to that of models trained on larger datasets with no data transfer, indicating that small-scale, independent datasets can be highly representative of the underlying distribution. We also explore the relationship between the quality of data and participation, discovering that users contributing larger datasets tend to do so at the expense of others, highlighting a potential limitation of the current data structure. To address this constraint, we present an innovative approach called FedHealth*, which incorporates a scoring system to evaluate participant data quality and adjusts the learning rate accordingly. As a result, FedHealth* promotes more balanced participation and accelerates the convergence of learning across all users. Source code is available at https://github.com/yousefishere/FedHealth. Finally, we provide an application example for FedHealth, where it is applied to schedule physical activity across all participants. The optimized model is made available at https://yousefishere.github.io/schedule/. Additionally, we include an analysis of our method's security and privacy properties. To resolve it, LQs with a mass difference of less than 300 GeV or a combined mass below 1 TeV are required. Ultra-thin gas layers within galaxies' central regions pose an unresolved problem in astrophysics. A key question concerns the heating mechanisms that prevent these gas layers from cooling below a certain threshold, even when they are not involved in active nuclear phenomena. A seemingly insignificant stimulation of the molecular gas's internal rotation might be the answer, potentially useful as a measure of the total mass of molecular gas in galaxies. A statistical analysis of 25 galaxies shows a strong correlation between this stimulation and the total mass of molecular gas, while the effect of other factors such as galaxy interaction, luminosity, and black hole mass is minimal. A simple analytical model demonstrates that this stimulation can be an effective non-invasive indicator of the total mass of molecular gas and gas surface density. However, it is also influenced by gas layers with high vertical scales, distinguishing it from the relationship predicted by global galaxy dynamics. A more precise understanding of these gas layers is crucial for improving our knowledge of galaxy evolution and mass regulation. Classifying musical devices, such as instruments from audio clips, has historically been challenging for existing methods and requires highly specialized features. A new technique has emerged that uses hierarchical frameworks to recognize new classes from limited data, and we're exploring its potential by applying this method to musical device detection. We create three new datasets that combine parent and child categories in a hierarchical structure and use them to test a protocol that focuses on few-shot learning. The results show hierarchical features lead to better performance and ease in learning from limited data, and we observe similar improvements in real-world applications. Notably, we report the first few-shot accuracies in this domain of research. Furthermore, we find that our proposed method achieves comparable performance to finetuning but outperforms it in terms of efficiency. The code and datasets are available for public use. We also experiment with other types of relationships between classes and find that our proposed method is effective in most cases. The paper introduces a new task, few-shot musical device recognition, and we believe it has potential applications in a range of areas, including entertainment and education. Intelligent machines are increasingly relying on neural networks for their decision-making processes but often lack a clear understanding of the underlying mechanisms. As they incorporate new information, their neural networks undergo changes, affecting their behavior. This process of updating the network is known as neural learning. It is crucial to anticipate the effects of contextual cues on these changes, particularly when they lead to biased adaptations. This phenomenon of causal neural learning enables machines to anticipate how they will learn from experience, but it also introduces novel challenges in both machine learning and cognitive science. This survey paper provides a multi-faceted analysis of this process, starting from the machine learning perspective, where it's seen as a complex problem of optimization, but also from a cognitive perspective, where it involves navigating the interplay between representation, computation, and variation in neural networks. This dual perspective reveals that biases in the network are often a result of the interplay between its capacity for flexible representation and its computational properties. This has significant implications for the design of machines that can learn from experience, especially when it comes to dealing with issues of causality, rationality, and the natural variability present in complex data. This survey paper also introduces a new framework that captures the essence of causal neural learning, but solving these machine learning problems also raises fundamental questions about the machines' understanding of themselves and their place in the world. The true risk of being hit by a car when crossing the street or waiting at a bus stop is often underestimated. A key factor contributing to this misperception is the tendency to overestimate one's own ability to avoid misfortunes. To investigate this dynamic, a theoretical model is developed, which demonstrates that individuals' propensity for self-serving biases can lead to an excessive willingness to take risks and, conversely, their reluctance to impose risks on others. To test these concepts in a real-world setting, a survey was conducted among pedestrians and was designed to be free of any influence from their self-image. The findings support the idea that self-serving biases play a significant role in how individuals evaluate risks of being hit by a car. Furthermore, it was observed that pedestrians' risk assessment varies greatly depending on the specific scenario, which raises important implications for the communication of risk information. The issue at hand is particularly relevant due to the widespread use of infrastructure risk assessment tools that rely on statistics that are often outdated or misleading. To address this challenge, a novel approach is presented that can provide a dynamic perspective on risk by incorporating real-time traffic data. The method is evaluated through a survey among pedestrians, which shows that their risk assessment is highly influenced by their self-image but is significantly reduced when they are made aware of the actual risks. Interestingly, even when the actual risks are presented without any reference to their own safety habits, pedestrians are still willing to take more risks than would be expected, which indicates the presence of self-serving biases in all scenarios. Which raises the question whether it would be beneficial to incorporate a margin of error when communicating risk information to the general public. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency sound wave bending phenomena. However, actual implementation of these concepts is hindered by existing fabrication methods' limitations. We introduce a novel method for mass-producing microacoustic BAF components via two-photon lithography, enabling precise creation of sub-wavelength structures in polydimethylglowane monomers with sound frequencies exceeding 100 kHz. As an example, a miniaturized acoustic BAF metagrating is designed and manufactured with reduced unit cells through simulation-activated recording, and its bending properties are verified at 120 kHz, demonstrating successful application of this technique. Furthermore, simulation and testing confirm that this method can generate coherent acoustic waves with up to 80% efficiency. We also examine the effects of different unit cell arrangements and their connections on acoustic performance. This breakthrough in low-cost, high-resolution fabrication of microacoustic components via two-photon lithography presents a viable pathway for developing complex acoustic metamaterials in the ultra-high frequency range. As this method combines the precision of advanced simulation tools with the efficiency of mass production, it is particularly well-suited for emerging applications involving high-frequency sound, such as medical imaging and non-destructive testing. However, the development of this method is not without its challenges, as increasing the frequency further leads to a sudden loss of bending phenomenon, which is attributed to a changing phase velocity that exceeds the group velocity of sound. Therefore, there is a need to revisit the theoretical basis of BAF physics and consider new strategies for designing and fabricating microacoustic components that can handle frequencies beyond 100 kHz. Nonetheless, this work provides a ground-breaking opportunity for re-examining acoustic wave dynamics in the ultra-high frequency range and exploring new possibilities for sound manipulation. High-frequency sound is highly sensitive to vibration, which poses significant diffusion and recording challenges. As a result, the best way to capture it is through vibration-sensing technology. Furthermore, the high-frequency sound spectrum is largely under the control of vibration parameters, which means that tight control over these parameters is essential to optimizing the sound experience. To achieve this, we propose a data-driven approach that leverages machine learning to efficiently search for the most critical vibration factors influencing sound at extremely high frequencies. Through this method, we are able to substantially reduce the dimensionality of our search from hundreds of variables to just a few key factors, which can be precisely controlled through vibration engineering to deliver the ultimate sound experience. A comprehensive mathematical model for both linear and nonlinear interaction of modes in optical resonators and waveguides has been developed, incorporating Kerr nonlinearity. Kerr nonlinearity leads to mode coupling, which results in the expansion of mode evolution and enables the identification of additional solutions, including those related to optical shock waves and solitons. This model is applicable to various geometries and is particularly relevant to photonic crystal structures. It demonstrates the possibility of soliton formation in certain environments and highlights the importance of carefully selecting the width of waveguides to stabilize solitons. Furthermore, the model indicates that increasing the depth of a defect in a photonic crystal structure or the intensity of an external electric field will either enhance soliton stability or trigger the formation of optical shock waves. Additionally, it shows that decreasing the width of a guide will either increase the amplitude of solitons or stabilize them. This model also facilitates the identification of solitons in waveguides with a narrow width and demonstrates that decreasing the width of a guide will either stabilize solitons or result in the formation of optical shock waves. It is demonstrated that both a decrease in the width of a guide or an increase in the depth of a defect in a photonic crystal structure or the intensity of an external electric field will either enhance soliton stability or trigger the formation of optical shock waves. Additionally, the paper introduces a novel method for determining the convergence and stability of a system on its boundary through the creation of a convergent and stable operator on a limitless domain. This technique is subsequently applied to several regulation systems with boundary constraints, including the control of an aircraft, a mobile robot, and a mechanical system with rotating wheels, by translating their boundary constraints into a limitless domain of controls. These conversions enable the construction of a Lyapunov function to prove the convergence and stability of these systems. This approach is particularly suited for discussing the effects of rough controls on a system's continuity and the implications for a system's stability. Many cutting-edge reinforcement learning projects originate from games, yet existing tools primarily focus on visual games, neglecting text-based games. We introduce L2Explorer, a comprehensive, text-based evaluation platform that integrates diverse sources, including the GameWiki, BookWiki, and ClassicRPG datasets, featuring over 200 intricate worlds. L2Explorer offers multiple challenging tasks, allows for infinite, dynamically generated levels in each domain, and incorporates multiple evaluation metrics, including automated assessment and human validation. To facilitate seamless reinforcement learning development, L2Explorer provides intuitive tools for transparent observation information, predefined reward functions, and intuitive interfaces for efficient data annotation. We believe L2Explorer to be a groundbreaking platform, capable of propelling the advancement of reinforcement learning through the creation of generalizable artificial worlds. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and explore the vast possibilities offered by L2Explorer. To accelerate the development of cross-language sentiment analysis, this paper introduces a novel multi-task training approach that combines tasks across languages. Existing methods typically train models on a single task and language at a time, but this proposal leverages relevant tasks in other languages to enhance the accuracy of sentiment analysis. A key innovation is the design of a shared task-aware attention mechanism, which enables models to selectively focus on relevant information from related tasks. Another important feature is a task-routing mechanism, which strategically assigns models to specific tasks based on their strengths. Through experiments, the benefits of this multi-task framework are demonstrated, resulting in improvements of up to 6.86% in accuracy for zero-shot cross-language sentiment classification. Moreover, this approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods for single-language sentiment analysis and significantly outperforms the baseline in few-shot scenarios. Additionally, this paper observes that, for some language pairs, the data available for training are rather imbalanced, comprising mostly neutral sentences. A notable example is the Dutch-English pair, where only around 5% of the available data consist of sentiment-labeled sentences. This characteristic poses a significant challenge for models trained on such datasets, as they often struggle to recognize the sentiment expressed in positive or negative sentences. A key observation made in this paper is the disparity in the distribution of sentiment scores, as shown in Figure 1, where the Dutch-English dataset visibly lags behind other cross-language datasets. This issue calls for innovative solutions that cater to low-frequency sentiment expressions in certain language pairs. The current leading method for visual association detection, using a two-stage approach with image-classification networks in both proposal generation and refinement stages, is fundamentally flawed due to its inability to accurately assess associations between objects. This limitation is exacerbated by the presence of misleading positive examples which mislead models and impede progress in developing effective association detectors. To tackle this issue, a novel approach called Association-aware Cross-Entropy (ACE) is proposed, focusing on enhancing the image-classification based framework by integrating object-association context. By associating each proposed box with a specific object and assessing their connection through a relational bridge, ACE modifies the standard cross-entropy objective function to include association information. This results in a more robust model in dealing with misleading positive examples, leading to a relative improvement of 14.2% in mean average precision (AP) on the VGG-Face-VAE dataset and 12.3% on the CUB-200-2011 dataset over the traditional two-stage approach. Moreover, ACE demonstrates exceptional generalization skills, achieving a notable AP increase of 18.9% on the CUB-200-2011 dataset when trained and evaluated with different datasets. To facilitate model evaluation and comparison, a revised evaluation protocol is proposed, along with comprehensive experiments and a comprehensive comparison with the state-of-the-art methods. This includes a notable result of ACE outperforming the leading methods by a significant margin on the CUB-200-2011 dataset, achieving an AP of 34.5%. To ensure the reproducibility of the results, the source code of the proposed method has been made publicly available. On November 4, 2004, a significant X8.0 solar flare occurred, followed by a massive coronal mass ejection that impacted Earth on November 4-5, 2004. Despite initial readings indicating elevated neutron counts, subsequent validation showed the event's neutron production was actually very low, likely due to energetic protons masking the signal. Using detailed data from the neutron detectors on board the MIPAS and AIM instruments, as well as the SOLAR mission, we developed a method to subtract the protons' influence, revealing the true impact of solar neutrons on Earth's atmosphere. By applying this technique to data from the time in question, November 7, 2004, we discovered that the previously masked signal of solar neutrons indeed matched expectations, with a calculated integral flux of approximately 41 x 10^8 (cm^2 s sr). Moreover, the data indicated an average decomposition lifetime of about 4.4 days for the 14.5 MeV neutrons, with a small standard deviation, indicating a minor degree of variation. This research is significant because it highlights the difficulty in detecting solar neutrons due to the overwhelming presence of other energetic particles, and our novel approach may be useful for uncovering other masked signals elsewhere in the data set. Additionally, it offers key insights into the decay behavior of solar neutrons, which could be linked to their breakdown within the atmosphere over extended time frames. Furthermore, our analysis raises the intriguing possibility that the apparent disparity in measured and calculated neutron fluxes could be an issue of time-dependent decomposition, which may need to be adjusted based on specific meteorological conditions and/or solar event characteristics. Lastly, our study suggests that the MIPAS/AIM detector's sensitivity may be sufficient to detect the decomposition's effects over several days, providing a foundation for exploring this phenomenon further with a more advanced detector in future missions. This high rotation rate suggests the planet may be experiencing substantial tidal heating. However, observations indicate the planet's equatorial surface is subjected to intense illumination for extended periods, potentially counteracting its angular momentum and slowing its spin. Furthermore, calculations reveal the planet's facade likely suffers significant absorption due to its being constantly illuminated by the star, possibly exceeding 150 times the Earth's atmospheric energy absorption from the sun. This energy absorption, likely caused by atmospheric loss or an unforeseen angular momentum transfer process, could be responsible for slowing the planet's spin and distorting its orbit. Observations with the Hubble Space Telescope can aid in verifying these findings and understanding the planet's environmental characteristics. Additionally, modeling by the BandedMap tool shows the possible existence of extensive cloud bands on the planet, which could be illuminated due to their three-week orbital period. This, however, would not fully explain the observed facade heating, accounting for less than half of the energy absorbed. It is crucial to validate the findings on K2-22b to determine their general applicability, as the planet represents a relatively small size in the sample of large exoplanets. It is also essential to consider that the effects seen in K2-22b might be representative of those experienced by other massive exoplanets located near their host stars' habitable zones. It is also essential to determine whether the angular momentum transfer process that slows the spin of K2-22b is a widespread phenomenon. A computational model employing biophysical principles has been developed to understand the underlying causes of Parkinson's disease.  Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder affecting movement control, results from the death of midbrain dopamine neurons.  Our model, centering on the primate brain, focuses on the interactions between dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatal neurons.  It incorporates the impact of missing dopamine on the functioning of striatal neurons and the resulting abnormality in movement-related brain areas.  To validate the model, we simulated a Parkinson's disease state and compared the results to actual brain activity measurements obtained from magnetencephalography in marmoset monkeys with induced Parkinson's-like symptoms.  The model successfully replicated the distinct changes in brain function associated with Parkinson's disease.  It also demonstrated the time-dependent effects of declining dopamine levels on brain function, supporting the idea that early intervention may yield better outcomes for treating the movement-related symptoms of Parkinson's disease.  The model can be used to explore novel treatments for Parkinson's disease.  Furthermore, it may be applicable to humans because the similar brain function shared by primates makes the model a relevant tool for understanding human Parkinson's disease. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Cloud amounts play a crucial role in climate models and other geographical phenomena affecting regional climates.  Up until now, cloud amounts have relied on subjective estimates from satellite images, but deep learning methods can provide a more precise and unbiased measurement.  Our novel multi-class dataset, named CloudAmount (CA), contains 15,000 annotated images representing eight distinct cloud amounts, from "None" to "Overcast".  Due to a lack of identical and mirrored sky images, we developed a innovative enhancement algorithm, called SkyMirrorGen, that utilizes a trained StyleGAN to create spatially-coherent cloud images by reflecting certain components of existing images.  Our model, SkyMirrorGen, successfully generates highly accurate images containing various cloud amounts, even across different image sources.  When evaluated on the CA dataset with multiple Convolutional Neural Network architectures, our results show that cloud amount recognition performance is significantly impeded when using unenhanced and mirrored images.  Notably, our best-performing model achieves a remarkable 73% accuracy on the CA dataset, significantly surpassing previous studies.  Interestingly, we observe cloud amount recognition to be more challenging below 50% cloud coverage, and enhance this underperforming region with additional training data and a spatial-aware assessment framework.  With improved performance, our model reaches an impressive 75% accuracy in the difficult low-cloud-base scenario.  Our advancements in cloud amount recognition set a new benchmark for evaluating the capability of deep learning models to analyze complex global imagery.  Furthermore, our data augmentation technique, centered around SkyMirrorGen, becomes the leading approach to tackle great-related challenges, such as recognizing land cover, predicting global weather patterns, and estimating climate conditions, among others.  Consequently, we release our novel dataset, along with the source code of SkyMirrorGen, under an open-source framework, to facilitate further exploration and development of the field. Similarly, $f(R)$ gravity's ability to resist rapid changes in the cosmological constant can also have an effect on dark matter's distribution. The combination of these two factors may have a combined impact on the turn-around radius, which is often used as a measure of the scale of galaxy halos. The effects mentioned above can lead to a reduction in the turn-around radius due to dark matter's reduced density at the right hand side of the potential well, resulting in a decrease in the galaxy's mass at a given radius. This effect, however, may be masked by the influence of dark energy on the universe's expansion, which dominates at low matter densities. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in revolutionizing atmospheric circulation modeling. A key aspect of this approach involves using the Isaac transport algorithm to capture the interaction between distinct fluid layers within the atmosphere. To further develop this approach, it is essential to assess the accuracy of this algorithm in modeling convective processes. Using a single-column simulation with two interacting fluids, researchers aim to evaluate the Isaac algorithm's effectiveness in replicating Rayleigh-Benard convection both theoretically and through actual simulation. Their simulation consists of two horizontal layers of opposing temperature conditions, simulating the development of cellular convection when the Prandtl number is set at 0.71. We examine three different Jaynes-Cummings interactions between two separate, uncorrelated atoms and their respective cavities, seeking one that could genuinely entangle the atoms. A single round of interaction between the atoms and a shared classical laser field is not sufficient to achieve this goal. However, we find that both a cavity-cavity entanglement-assisting process and the application of a specific classical pulse can make it possible. Notably, the same classical pulse that fails to entangle the atoms when applied individually can successfully do so when they are combined with their respective cavities. Moreover, we demonstrate that a relatively weak intensity of the classical pulse, far below the saturation intensity, is already sufficient to achieve atom entanglement. Furthermore, we show that this weak classical pulse may also serve as a means to generate atom-field entanglement and steer the atom's motion. Lastly, we outline the necessary conditions for the classical pulse to efficiently produce atom entanglement, indicating that a relatively weak intensity could already meet these standards. Additionally, we find that one of the three JC models can result in durable atom entanglement, even with no applied classical pulse or requirement for cavity-cavity interaction. This finding holds significant implications for applying these results to actual experiments involving atoms that are not perfectly isolated from their surroundings. Overall, we believe that our findings could facilitate the development of novel applications for Jaynes-Cummings systems, such as the creation of atom-atom entanglement through a classical light field. This could enable the integration of JC systems with distinct connectivity, potentially enriching their collective quantum properties. Moreover, this integration could be achieved without the need for fragile atom-atom interactions or the assembly of complex quantum circuits. Instead, it would merely require the construction of multiple, separately accessible JC setups that can be simultaneously controlled with a single classical light field. This integrated approach to quantum technology could also provide a means to supplement the durability of atom entanglement, even in systems where the spontaneous emission plays a significant role. This could involve increasing the intensity of the classical light field to a point where the atom's response enters a saturation regime. Nonetheless, this approach holds significant challenges, primarily stemming from the extensive loss that occurs due to spontaneous emission, as well as the discontinuous nature of saturation, which could result in a failure to efficiently produce durable atom entanglement. Nonetheless, we find that another of the three JC models can overcome these difficulties, allowing for the generation of durable atom entanglement even when the atom's response does not enter a saturation regime

A method is presented for a scalar SU(2) glueball mass calculation, based on the interaction of gauge bosons represented in Weyl four-momentum space. The approach is systematic, and all terms in the spectral representation are equally important. Calculations are performed for the SU(2) theory in two dimensions using lattice QCD data for the lattice spacing and the mass gap value. The contribution from the Weyl four-momentum volume is found to be significant, and lattice QCD data cannot accurately determine it on their own. Once this volume effect is accounted for, a parametric approach yields reliable estimates for the spectral representation coefficients through a unitary matrix transformation. Further investigation of the SU(2) theory in two dimensions is recommended. The method proposed also extends to higher dimensions and may be applicable to other particle types. Additionally, the nature of particle states is reevaluated in quantum field theories, and it is argued that the overlap representation alone is insufficient for their description. Understanding public opinion on social media is crucial for businesses, governments, and other organizations to adjust their strategies effectively. Twitter, as a popular platform, offers a wealth of information about users' opinions, which can be difficult to pinpoint due to the presence of slang, abbreviations, and varying language use. Consequently, tracking the sentiment on Twitter becomes a complex task. This paper proposes an LSTM-based sentiment classification model that outperforms existing approaches by utilizing a diverse dataset of 9.5 million Twitter posts. To prepare the dataset for use, a novel preprocessing technique is introduced, which involves developing rules to identify and remove Twitter-specific information. This approach results in a more reliable dataset, free from noise, which in turn enhances the performance of the LSTM model. When evaluated against the cleaned dataset, the model achieves a sentiment accuracy of 80.7%, which represents a significant improvement over existing methods. To further validate the model's effectiveness, a comparison with five alternative approaches is conducted, revealing that it delivers the best accuracy among all candidates. This paper provides a comprehensive framework for sentiment classification on Twitter, which can be expanded to classify emotions such as anger, fear, and surprise. This classification achieves a good balance of precision and recall, outperforming all existing approaches while minimizing the influence of Twitter-specific information. This technique's applicability is not limited to sentiment analysis but can also be applied to other classification problems involving social media data. To facilitate replication, the dataset and model source code are made available for download. This approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through an experiment conducted over a prolonged period, spanning nearly three months. It shows that using a diverse dataset of Twitter posts results in a model with high accuracy, which is verified through a complementary experiment conducted concurrently. This paper introduces an innovative solution to sentiment assessment on Twitter, including a new preprocessing technique, a diverse dataset, and a model that achieves high accuracy through the use of word2vec and long-short-term memory (LSTM) techniques. This approach outperforms all existing methods while providing a clear explanation for the sentiment of each Twitter post. It provides a new perspective on sentiment analysis, emphasizing the importance of using a diverse dataset and thoroughly understanding Twitter-specific information to achieve accurate results. This paper's novel features include a diverse dataset of Twitter posts, a new preprocessing technique, and a model that uses word2vec and LSTM techniques to assess the sentiment of each post. It represents a major advancement in sentiment assessment on Twitter, providing a clear explanation for the sentiment of each post and outperforming all existing methods.

This research investigates the amphibian model, a probabilistic process that uses a binary tree to determine the reliability of a component consisting of multiple sub-systems. We are particularly interested in identifying the critical density required for the process to converge, as this has implications for assessing the reliability of systems at the intersection of discrete and continuous scales. By analyzing the characteristics of the amphibian model and modifying it to incorporate a variant of the Harris-Chung boundary condition, we are able to determine the critical density at approximately 2.59. This finding suggests that the amphibian model converges when the edge density of the binary tree is in the range of 2.51 to 2.67. This result demonstrates that the critical density of the amphibian model is closely correlated with the extent of a binary tree. Furthermore, this correlation implies that the reliability of systems composed of sub-components, as they transition from a discrete to a continuous distribution, is heavily influenced by the degree of the tree. Additionally, this correlation serves as a method for validating the results obtained from the modified Harris-Chung boundary condition. Additionally, we are also exploring ways to incorporate the amphibian model with regard to the geometry of a k-ary tree. This modification may provide a means to analyze systems that feature a tree-like structure in $d$-dimensional space, particularly in regards to the critical density required for convergence. However, this research remains an open problem at this time. This research was initially discussed at the 2019 Wilson Conference on Statistical Mechanics. Moreover, the recent work on the amphibian model was presented at the 2020 Online Special Session of the Wilson Conference on Statistical Mechanics.

In conclusion, the critical density for the amphibian model is the extent of a binary tree. This has significant implications for assessing the reliability of systems at the intersection of discrete and continuous scales.

Imitation learning is a strong technique for training optimal policies, but its effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of the demonstrated behaviors. When the supplied transitions contain significant errors, the usual imitation learning approach can result in a policy that is far inferior to its source. To tackle this challenge, we limit the impact of defective transitions by reducing the influence of the expert on regions with low density in the state space. This strategic relaxation allows us to develop an algorithm called TRAIL that leverages a combination of expert demonstrations and self-exploration to identify areas with high density and learn a close-to-ideal policy within them. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that TRAIL achieves a balance between the effect of the expert and that of the data, resulting in a policy that is close to optimal despite containing some density-based biases. We support our claims with a range of experiments showcasing the superior performance of TRAIL in comparison to conventional imitation learning methods. The code for our study has been made publicly available on GitHub. Large-scale neural machine translation systems typically utilize attention-based models to significantly reduce the number of possible source sentence positions that need to be generated during each inference. Nonetheless, the model still needs to predict every possible target word given the current context, making the action space extensive. Recent studies suggest that search-based methods with limited action spaces can achieve higher quality translations. Therefore, we propose a novel framework that combines search-based methods with attention-based generation for both source and target. Our goal is to explore the potential of using reinforcement learning to improve translation quality when the action space is extensive. Experimentally, our results show that learning the model's parameters can lead to a significant 11% improvement in BLEU scores for long target sentences on the WMT'14 English-to-German test set, suggesting that this approach may effectively address the issue of target sentence length. Our model, however, still underperforms human translators by a substantial 6% BLEU scores. To further investigate this, we find that a significant issue with our reinforcement learning method is the difficulty it faces in processing long target sentences due to the requirement for sentence-level rewards. This constraint leads to very slow training, resulting in poor translations and significantly impairs the ability of our model to learn from these predictions. As a result, our scores fall short of human standards, translating only to a 5.5% improvement at the WMT'14 English-to-German test set. To handle this problem, we introduce two innovative solutions: first, we train and evaluate our model on character-level data, removing the requirement for sentence-level rewards and reducing training time by a factor of 30; second, we introduce a novel double-learning method, learning two models in parallel and applying the knowledge from the model that has seen more data to the model that has seen less data. This method proves particularly effective when comparing the results for source and target sentences of different lengths. Our research also offers some practical strategies for breaking down the "filter bubbles," such as promoting users to actively seek out content that contradicts their predefined interests. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that is increasingly part of critical information systems requiring high integrity. To assure such integrity, it is essential to validate transactions for consistency. However, detecting anomalies in MongoDB's distributed, document-oriented transactions is complex due to its non-linear representation of data. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach to create a linearized representation of transactions that enables us to leverage established methods for anomaly detection. Our approach involves converting MongoDB transactions into a composite data structure called a transaction graph and using it to create a linearized version called a dotted graph. We propose a new algorithm, called Dotted-Reachability-Table (DRT), that determines reachability in the dotted graph and prove its correctness. Furthermore, we compare the efficiency of DRT with existing methods, demonstrating its superiority. To validate our approach, we conduct a real-world evaluation of our DRT algorithm alongside a reference implementation for MongoDB. Our experimental results show that our approach is not only feasible but also yields impressive performance gains. To facilitate replication, we make our evaluation data and methodology publicly available. Our work introduces a groundbreaking method for validating MongoDB transactions and sets a significant benchmark for similar distributed, document-oriented database systems. To build upon this foundation, we invite the research community to contribute to the further development of transaction validation techniques in such databases. Our work is a landmark achievement in the field of database research, and we look forward to collaborating with experts to push the boundaries of innovation. With the ever-expanding use of NoSQL databases in various domains, there is an increasing need for efficient transaction validation methods that can ensure data integrity. Our solution provides a practical answer to this need and can be used to develop reliable software applications that leverage MongoDB in their data storage layer. Additionally, we establish an intriguing connection between these results and certain inverse Kostka numbers. Further investigation into these numbers reveals their representation through a natural set of tableaux, which we term 'inverse Kostka tableaux'. These tableaux not only provide an intuitive explanation for the results related to chromatic symmetric polynomials but also suggest a broader algebraic framework. Finally, we introduce the concept of 'dual buzzinews', an intricate algebraic construct, which is closely related to inverse Kostka tableaux and likely holds significance in the broader theory of symmetric function theory. We also make the computational tool 'RotaWalk', available online, which enables interactive exploration of these intricate mathematical structures. Specifically, it allows users to visualize, manipulate, and compute various objects related to classical Young diagrams, symmetric function basis expansion, recurrence coefficients, moment matrices, and more, all while providing a comprehensive framework that encompasses not just our current results, but also a vast range of diverse topics within symmetric function and multivariate approximation theory. We invite fellow mathematicians to engage with this intellectual treasure trove and invite suggestions for additional features to be incorporated into this versatile computational tool. We firmly believe that our results related to chromatic symmetric polynomials, inverse Kostka numbers, and the associated walk and tree structures, collectively referred to as the 'buzznews package', have the potential to significantly impact future research in the field of algebra and mathematics. We are confident that our findings, particularly those related to positivity and multivariate approximation, will continue to be relevant and worthwhile for scholars to study and build upon in the years to come. We anticipate that the availability of the computational tool, 'RotaWalk', will provide a valuable resource for both established professionals and young academics, offering them a chance to explore the intricacies of these complex mathematical constructs and perhaps most importantly, to be inspired by the beautiful and elegant nature of the underlying mathematics. The standard approach in medical image analysis, known as group-wise processing, assumes images with similar clinical characteristics share the same statistical properties. However, this assumption is invalidated when there are intrinsic biases present. Current methods that aim to detect and eliminate intrinsic biases in medical image sets fail to address two key issues: accurately identifying biases in data and properly normalizing data without introducing new biases. To address these challenges, we propose a new point-wise method that relies solely on analyzing individual image pairs. This approach involves developing two novel bias detection metrics, based on entropy and energy measures, that can be applied without relying on comparative studies or assuming knowledge of reference densities. Our results demonstrate that these metrics are efficient in identifying biased images and outperform existing methods. Our study stresses the necessity to develop rigorous evaluation protocols, adaptive comparison methods, and replication guidelines for analyzing medical image analysis tasks. Research on complex systems from the human brain to protein structures within cells yields exponential probability distributions when analyzing the number of components in each substructure. This phenomenon can be explained by applying a geometric model that represents interacting components as points in a 2D space, where nearby elements with short distances are more likely to form bonds. When elements with short distances are prevented from bonding, the distribution changes to a uniform pattern. This discovery can be taken a step further by limiting the space to an equilateral triangle, dividing it into smaller triangles, and varying the energy costs associated with breaking bonds within each section. When applying this concept to nanoscale assemblies composed of iron atoms, their spatial arrangements and magnetic properties can be understood, and even how they change over time. This knowledge can be utilized to control and manipulate these systems with spin reversal dynamics. This approach is not confined to magnetic interactions but can be applied to any type of geometric relationship, making it a versatile method for analyzing complex systems. Speech emotion recognition is a key aspect in developing realistic computer characters, and achieving this aims to create a more immersive gaming experience. This task is complicated by the limited size and low-quality datasets commonly associated with speech emotion recognition. Our research extracts audio features using a deep neural network, and refines them through speech emotion recognition tasks on two adapted datasets from the Internet, significantly reducing the necessary training data by a factor of ten. Notably, our model performs notably better than a comparable baseline, achieving a 13% improvement in accuracy. Additionally, our findings indicate strong potential for applying domain adaptation to emit diverse character personalities. To further explore this idea, we introduce an innovative approach called the 'Multi-Adaptation Character Framework', which involves adapting our core speech emotion recognition model for each character through a mini-domain adaptation process, and demonstrates promising results in an evaluation study. The code is now openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

We examine the measurement-based description of a system that interacts between light and matter, and we highlight the differences between two approaches: a microscopic one and a macroscopic one. While the macroscopic approach is straightforward for electromagnetic fields described by linear dipole responses, things become more complex when we consider higher-order measurements or those that are not linear. In such cases, the macroscopic approach relies on an empirical measurement operator that is derived from a linearized process, yet this can still yield accurate results when used in a non-linear process. We demonstrate this by applying our arguments to an example involving light-matter interactions in second-order processes, and we show that the empirical measurement operator can also be used in models that incorporate spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we find that the choice of measure has no impact on the behavior of systems that interact with light, as long as the measure is compatible with the system's symmetries. Additionally, we discuss how to overcome potential issues with the empirical measurement operator that arises from using a measure that is not compatible with the system's symmetries. We expect that our findings will be particularly useful for researchers who are constructing quantum simulators with light-matter interactions. We also propose that the issue of choosing a suitable measure should be addressed before it becomes a major concern in the field. In the meantime, we believe that researchers should prioritize experimenting with different measures in their research. We hope that our work will serve as an inspiration to the next generation of researchers who will push the boundaries of what is possible with quantum simulations. Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective disaster response information dissemination. Social media networks can provide valuable insights into public perception, albeit limited by constrainted access and temporal relevance. A no-hypothesis approach was employed to explore Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake and analyze accompanying videos featuring early warning signs, with findings indicating a mere 1.3% of relevant tweets also included video content. Approximately 11% of tweets containing videos were posted within the first hour after the quake, with this group being the most active in sharing videos. The most prevalent video features were related to shaking and fugitive waves, with 57% of annotated videos meeting the study's content standards. 85% of these annotated videos were posted by users with over 500 followers, with 21% originating from international users. The majority of annotated videos were recorded within 5000 meters of the earthquake's epicenter and had a 70% chance of being captured within 2000 meters. A model assessing the validity of Twitter data identified 72% of annotated videos as credible, with the remaining 28% being classified as unverified or disinformation. These results demonstrate the value of Twitter data, including accompanying videos, in promoting public awareness about earthquakes. This paper investigates key properties of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which serve as the highest smoothness requirements for functions to be Fourier transformable and differentiable to infinity. We explore how Fourier transform-based descriptions can vary significantly depending on whether these spaces are ordinary or extraordinary. This distinction holds important implications, particularly in the context of Toeplitz operators. Although Toeplitz operators are generally well-defined on ordinary Gelfand-Shilov spaces, we demonstrate that this definition is insufficient when dealing with extraordinary spaces. Consequently, our findings imply that many results cited in other studies are inaccurate. Moreover, we identify a crucial condition that influences the continuity of Toeplitz operators when defined on extraordinary Gelfand-Shilov spaces. Additionally, we establish that Banach spaces of functions, which satisfy specific growth conditions and smoothness requirements, can be equivalently defined using Fourier transform-based descriptions. Furthermore, we establish connections between Banach spaces of functions that satisfy condition (C) and smooth Gelfand-Shilov spaces. Lastly, we conclude this paper by discussing potential areas for further research. This paper is a revised and expanded version of our previous paper, which was previously posted online. Since then, we have incorporated additional corrections, including fixing an error in Theorem 2.3, which was previously stated in its incorrect form as Theorem 2.1. Additionally, we have addressed concerns raised by Professor P. R. Popescu. His input proved particularly beneficial in helping us clarify the non-ordinary nature of Banach spaces of functions that satisfy condition (C). We would like to express our gratitude to Professor Popescu for his insights and contributions. His input enabled us to refine the characterization of Banach spaces of functions that satisfy condition (C), which are smooth in the sense of Gelfand-Shilov. We would also like to take the opportunity to correct an earlier statement, which stated that distributional smoothness is a more relaxed condition than smoothness in the sense of Gelfand-Shilov. While this statement holds true for finite smoothness requirements, it is not applicable to infinite smoothness requirements. Conversely, smoothness in the sense of Gelfand-Shilov is a more relaxed condition than distributional smoothness. We hope that these corrections will be beneficial in furthering the development of research related to Gelfand-Shilov spaces. We would like to take the opportunity to express our gratitude to Professor K. Toda for bringing to our attention an error in the publication of our previous paper

Conversely, introducing a defect in a PT-symmetric unit cell or a PT-phased defect in a non-PT symmetric unit cell both serve to increase the coherent flawless point and reduce wave transmission clarity in a PT-symmetric periodic network. Our findings may contribute to the development of PT-symmetric photonics, a relatively new field. This universal representation facilitates the computation of matrix elements in any HFB wave function, regardless of its complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fundamental properties of HFB wave functions, such as overlap and coherence, can be effectively computed utilizing this universal representation, leading to a clearer physical interpretation. Additionally, we show that the universal representation is invaluable for simplifying complex HFB configurations, enabling us to recover important physical characteristics, including quasiparticle energies and densities, even in multi-quasiparticle configurations. This leads to a better understanding of how the interactions between quasiparticles influence physical properties. Three-dimensional point clouds are increasingly being used in visual navigation tasks, but their representations suffer from fluctuations due to the accumulation of errors from sensor readings and image projections, which limits current optimization techniques in navigation applications. To address this challenge, a new approach called Transformation-Dependent Smoothing is proposed, which takes the transformation history into account when smoothing 3D point clouds. This method uses a novel graph neural network architecture that incorporates transformation information to produce more accurate representations of the environment, leading to better performance in visual navigation tasks. Our proposed technique is efficient, lightweight, and straightforward to integrate with existing navigation systems, and it has been effectively applied to the ODE-SL framework. Experimental results show that this method outperforms existing optimization techniques and improves the performance of visual navigation tasks. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for inferring accurate event and timeline information. Existing techniques primarily focus on incorporating time information into their representation models, using techniques such as temporal embedding and time-agnostic attention mechanisms. In contrast, we propose a novel, model-independent approach that leverages time information through low-rank representations. We based our framework on the observation that time and entity representations are intertwined and intersecting factors that together encompass all possible instances and time periods. Consequently, we adopted a factorized framework that decomposes time and entity representations into their primal components, thereby enabling the capture of complex temporal patterns through the integration of time representations. Moreover, this approach automatically yields a combined representation that integrates both time and entity information. We evaluated our approach using a recently introduced dataset focused on temporal timeline inference and found it to achieve superior results when compared to various benchmark models. Moreover, we found that our approach facilitates compact and interpretable representations that reflect the temporal relationships stated in the knowledge graph. Notably, our approach results in entity and time representations that are independent of the model used, as evidenced by the fact that our scores remain consistent across different models. We believe this to be a critical aspect of temporal knowledge graph completion, as it enables the use of advanced machine learning techniques that further improve the accuracy of inference. We anticipate that our approach will also be applicable to event and timeline datasets that focus on event participation, timeline ordering, and temporal anchoring. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw2/lowrank-tkg. Additionally, we have introduced an improved version of the AIO dataset, which includes additional truth labels for the event participation task. This updated dataset can be downloaded at https://github.com/hjdw2/lowrank-tkg/tree/main/data. Moreover, we found that our approach is well-suited for incorporating time expertise through the use of time-specific instances. dimensionality reduction technique, known as t-distributed dimensionality
reduction, and builds upon it by incorporating the direction and
magnitude of feedforward connections in a neural network. This approach is
efficiently integrated with clustering algorithms, allowing IBC to identify
distinct groups within complex data sets, as demonstrated through the analysis

data. Notably, IBC's performance surpasses that of comparison algorithms, including
ones employing advanced dimensionality reduction methods, such as Autoencoders

than existing algorithms. Additionally, IBC is found to be robust to the initial conditions used to initiate the neural network and the localization of the number of clusters.

Interstellar panspermia, a theoretical concept suggesting microbial life forms can thrive during exposure to space across star systems, is evaluated in terms of viability based on the characteristics of celestial bodies and radiation levels in various astrophysical environments.  By considering factors such as the spectrum of electromagnetic radiation, temperatures in the microbial realm, and the transport of cometary ices, a comprehensive assessment is carried out for potential habitats in our solar system, as well as on exoplanets capable of supporting life and residing in close proximity to their host stars.  Our analysis indicates that only a limited set of habitats in our solar system can facilitate the survival of microbial life forms through exposure to space over an estimated 4.5 billion years.  Similarly, a restricted pool of Earth-like planets located near their host stars and capable of maintaining temperatures between -10°C and 50°C in the microbial realm will allow for the possible transport of viable microorganisms through interstellar dust particles over the desired time frame.  Furthermore, we establish that only a limited set of celestial bodies in the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud can serve as effective reservoirs for extropic microbial life to survive on over Gyr timescales, with these regions becoming accessible again in about 1 Gyr into the future due to the expansion of the solar system.  Lastly, we provide an informal argument that endozoic microfossils could be released back into space through the collapse of dying stars, thereby creating a potential link between the origins of life on Earth and other celestial bodies.  Finally, we propose that future experimental research on extreme forms of microbial life could offer a basis for developing viable indicators for interstellar panspermia, as well as provide useful guidelines for establishing policy frameworks that protect potential life forms transported back to our solar system following the collapse of dying stars.
